title: Learning is ok. The curriculum isn't.
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton argues that the essential nature of learning, a brain process of neuronal chains becoming sticky through repeated experience, will not change, but curriculums must. He starts with coding, once a curriculum star and now fading as AI writes its own code, and adds driver education and medical diagnosis as examples where technology has changed what people need to learn. Curriculums assume a stable, knowable future, an assumption now broken by the speed of AI development. Drawing on Camilla Cavendish's Financial Times piece, he suggests core aims such as adaptability, learning to fail and independent thinking alongside kindness and respect. He frames this as a rebalancing from knowledge-rich toward skills-capable, evolutionary for already broad schools and harder for those wedded to knowledge acquisition, while acknowledging that others will disagree.
points: Learning itself remains constant because it is a brain process, whereas curriculum is a declaration about what to learn and is already overloaded and partly out of date.
Curriculum depends on an agreed picture of the kind of person a school wants to develop, and AI is forcing that picture to be rethought.
A fluid curriculum without fixed content is unrealistic because assessment needs consistency, schools lack the expertise to switch quickly and parents want security.
Cavendish's list of adaptability, learning to fail, independent thinking and kindness is used to argue for rebalancing rather than abandoning knowledge.
He expects change to be evolutionary in schools already balancing skills and knowledge and slowly revolutionary for knowledge-acquisition cultures.
quotes: Our brains will make sure of that. It’s why learning is/should be our Hedgehog concept. Learning is always going to be here.
It is already overloaded. It already asks children and students to learn things that aren’t true. It already asks for too much coverage and not enough learning. It is, in part, already out of date.

An assumption has always been built into many curriculums that we live in a stable society and we know, more or less, what the future will look like. When we think we know what the future will look like we are able to describe more easily the kinds of people we want to help develop. We ‘know’ what knowledge, skills and understanding are needed.

Assessment and evaluation depend on a consistency around which judgements can be made and comparisons can happen. Schools don’t have - have never had - the expertise to switch quickly. Parents want some sense of security about the preparedness of their children’s futures, even if it is mis-placed.
I’m definitely not saying this. We may be asking for a) a rebalancing and b) a change in our fundamental purpose.

What we need is going to be an evolution for those schools and cultures already thinking broadly. It will need to be slowly revolutionary for those schools and cultures wedded strongly to a knowledge acquisition model.
Learning isn’t going to change. Right now, the curriculum has to. We need to get ready.
